Oral medicine and dentistry · published research

Local-anesthetic injection pain

Several pediatric randomized studies report less injection pain, though evidence is concentrated in specific procedures and age groups.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

Several pediatric randomized studies report less injection pain, though evidence is concentrated in specific procedures and age groups.

Summary of the Evidence

The exact dental-anesthesia category contains 33 unique titles: 20 human randomized reports, one nonrandomized study, one case report, and 11 reviews or syntheses. No animal or standalone in-vitro record is identified. Reviews summarize some of the same trials, and patient populations range from young children to adults. (Hamouda et al. 2024 Farah et al. 2025)

Human and clinical evidence

In a randomized trial of 64 children aged five to seven years, laser PBM was associated with lower pain indicators during local-anesthetic injection than topical anesthetic gel, without changing the effectiveness of anesthesia during subsequent dental procedures. A 2025 split-mouth study also reported less pain during inferior alveolar nerve block with 940 nm PBM. Results remain procedure-specific, and these findings do not establish efficacy across all injection sites or adult populations.

Animal evidence

No animal clinical or preclinical species study is indexed in the exact injection-pain category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study is identified in this category. Evidence concerns pain during clinical injections.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The cited 2025 study used a 940 nm near-infrared laser in a single session, with 4–6 J/cm² for 20 seconds. Other pediatric trials use different diode wavelengths, powers, and comparators, including topical anesthetic. Treatment sites and injection techniques vary, so the protocol should not be extrapolated without testing.

Interpretation

The evidence suggests that PBM may reduce injection discomfort in selected pediatric dental settings. Confidence is limited by small, heterogeneous trials and subjective outcomes. Future studies should prespecify age and injection site, compare with both sham and usual analgesia, report anesthetic success, and measure pain with validated scales and blinded assessment.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term injection-pain reduction in the studied procedures

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The category contains 33 titles, including 20 randomized reports and 11 reviews or syntheses. Trials differ in age group, injection method, topical anesthetic use, and pain scale. Further studies should use sham controls, standardized injection protocols, and consistent measures of pain and anesthetic efficacy.
